snippets.title: What counts as an e-bike in the EU
snippets.summary: A pedelec may assist only while you pedal, up to 25 km/h, with a motor rated at most 250 W continuous. Within those limits it is treated like a bicycle: no licence, insurance plate or helmet duty in Germany. Faster S-pedelecs (up to 45 km/h) need an insurance plate and a moped licence, and are banned from most cycle paths.

snippets.title: Hub motor or mid-drive under €1,500?
snippets.summary: Rear hub motors (typically 40–50 Nm) dominate this price band: quiet, cheap and low-maintenance, fine for flat city commutes. Mid-drives (50–85 Nm) climb far better because they use the bike's gears, but they wear chains faster and rarely appear below €1,400. If your route has sustained climbs above 6%, a mid-drive is worth stretching the budget for.

snippets.title: Battery size and real-world range
snippets.summary: Most models in this band carry 400–540 Wh. Expect roughly 40–70 km in mixed use on the middle assist level; the brochure figure usually assumes the lowest level, a light rider and flat roads. Cold weather cuts range by 20–30%. A removable battery lets you charge indoors, which also protects it in winter.

snippets.title: The hidden cost: replacing the battery
snippets.summary: Lithium-ion packs typically keep about 80% of their capacity after 500–1,000 full cycles. A replacement costs €350–650 in this segment, so check that the maker sells spare packs and that the warranty covers the battery for at least two years.

snippets.title: Brakes: why hydraulic discs matter
snippets.summary: An e-bike with rider weighs 100 kg or more and cruises at 25 km/h. Hydraulic disc brakes stop it predictably in the wet and need little adjustment; mechanical discs are acceptable on flat routes but fade on long descents. Avoid rim brakes on anything you will ride daily.

snippets.title: Weight and frame fit
snippets.summary: Budget e-bikes weigh 22–28 kg. If you carry the bike up stairs or onto trains, every kilogram counts; a folding model around 20 kg is the realistic option. Step-through frames are easier to mount with shopping on the rack. Always test-ride your size: a wrong frame costs more comfort than any spec difference.

snippets.title: Shortlist: six models under €1,500
snippets.summary: Voltra City 3 (€1,299, hub, 504 Wh), Kestrel Trail 500 (€1,449, mid-drive, 500 Wh), Nordwind Pendler (€1,199, hub, 417 Wh), Ampere Urban S (€1,379, hub, 540 Wh), Fjord Fold 20 (€1,099, folding, 360 Wh) and Riverline Step-Thru (€1,249, hub, 468 Wh). Market data for each is available at /api/market/:symbol.

snippets.title: Service network and warranty
snippets.summary: Online-only brands save €150–300 but can leave you without a local workshop for motor or display faults. Before buying, check that a shop within reach services the motor system, and that spare parts (display, controller, battery) are listed for at least five years.

snippets.title: Theft protection
snippets.summary: E-bikes are a favourite target for thieves. Budget for a solid lock (€60–120) and consider theft insurance; some insurers require a frame registration number and a lock of a certified security level. A removable battery also makes the bike less attractive to steal.

snippets.title: Five-year cost of ownership
snippets.summary: Over five years, plan for one battery (€350–650), two chains and cassettes (€120), brake pads and a yearly service (€300–400 in total) and a few euros of electricity per year. A €1,299 e-bike therefore costs roughly €2,100–2,500 to own, still far below a car or a monthly transit pass in most German cities.
